1296.title: Adab of travel
1296.hook: a verse for setting off, company on the road, and praise on the way home
1296.howItsDone: Muslims setting out on a journey say Allahu akbar and recite the verses of al-Zukhruf, "Glorified be He Who hath subdued these unto us," in Arabic, and on returning add words of praise.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adab of guests, and your line: honor the guest. Today the courtesy leaves the house with you.

The seatbelt clicks. The engine turns over. And before the car pulls out, the driver says a line under her breath, in Arabic. It isn't a line about cars. It comes from the Qur'an, from a passage about riding animals and ships, written long before any engine. Partway through, it admits something. It ends by mentioning a destination that isn't on any map in the car. Today: the manners of leaving home, and of coming back.
screen: `THE SEATBELT CLICKS.` → `A LINE BEFORE PULLING OUT.` → `A DESTINATION NOT ON THE MAP.`

segments.voice: Ibn 'Umar describes it in Sahih Muslim. When the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, mounted his camel to set out on a journey, he said Allahu akbar three times, then recited two verses of al-Zukhruf. In Pickthall's translation: "Glorified be He Who hath subdued these unto us, and we were not capable (of subduing them); And lo! unto our Lord we surely are returning." The admission first: we were not capable. The animal, the ship, today the car or the plane: none of it is ours by our own strength. Then the turn: unto our Lord we are returning. Every trip has a return built in, and the verse points past it to the last return of all. In the same report, he asked for goodness on the journey and for the distance to be made easy. Coming home, he said it again and added: returning, repenting, worshipping, praising our Lord. Two more pieces. Company: a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says, in paraphrase, that if people knew what he knew about traveling alone, no rider would travel alone at night. And home: another hadith in Bukhari calls travel a piece of torment, because it keeps a person from food, drink and sleep, so when your business is done, hurry back to your family. Leave remembering. Travel with others where you can. Come home quickly, praising.
screen: `WE WERE NOT CAPABLE OF IT.` · `UNTO OUR LORD WE ARE RETURNING.` · `NOT ALONE AT NIGHT.` · `DONE? HURRY HOME, PRAISING.`

segments.voice: Picture the next trip you'll take, even across town, and see yourself sitting down in the seat. If you pray, you can say the words now, in Arabic if you know them, or in English: Glorified be He Who hath subdued these unto us; if you don't, just notice how much of the trip you didn't build, the road, the engine, the hands that made them. Then see yourself walking back through your own door, and stay with that return.
Adab of travel. The manners of the road: remember Allah setting out, keep company where you can, and come home quickly, praising. Today's word.
Your line: travel remembering. Every trip has a return built in. Until tomorrow.

1297.title: Adab of sleep
1297.hook: the one thing no one can do on purpose, and the remembrance that goes with it
1297.howItsDone: Muslims follow the Prophet's bedtime practice: making wudu, lying on the right side, reciting al-Ikhlas, al-Falaq and al-Nas into cupped hands and wiping over the body, and saying "bismika Allahumma amutu wa ahya" before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adab of travel, and your line: travel remembering. Today, the shortest journey of every day: the one into sleep.

Lights off. Phone face down. And then the one thing in the day nobody can do on purpose: fall asleep. You can't push your way into it. You can only lie down and let go. The Qur'an treats that letting go as no small thing. In surah al-Zumar, in Pickthall's translation: "Allah receiveth (men's) souls at the time of their death, and that (soul) which dieth not (yet) in its sleep." Every night, something is handed over. Today: handing it over well.
screen: `LIGHTS OFF.` → `NOBODY FALLS ASLEEP ON PURPOSE.` → `EVERY NIGHT, A HANDING OVER.`

segments.voice: Start with al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, in Sahih al-Bukhari. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, told him, in paraphrase: when you go to your bed, make wudu as you would for prayer, lie down on your right side, and say a short du'a handing yourself over to Allah. Make it your last words, he said. If you die that night, you die on the fitrah, the natural state. The body washed, laid down a particular way, and the last words of the day chosen, not left to whatever was on the screen. Some of this you met on day one hundred thirty-six. Then 'A'ishah adds what she saw night after night, also in Bukhari: he cupped his hands, blew into them lightly, and recited the three short surahs at the end of the Qur'an, al-Ikhlas, al-Falaq and al-Nas, the three quls, each beginning with qul, say. Then he wiped his hands over as much of his body as he could, starting with his head and face, three times. Last, two sentences from Hudhayfah, in Bukhari. Lying down: in Your name, O Allah, I die and I live. Waking, in paraphrase: praise to Allah, who gave us life after He caused us to die, and to Him is the rising. Sleep, a small dying. Waking, a small rising. The verse from al-Zumar, folded into two lines a person can say in the dark.
screen: `WUDU, THEN THE RIGHT SIDE.` · `LAST WORDS, CHOSEN.` · `THREE QULS INTO CUPPED HANDS.` · `IN YOUR NAME I DIE AND I LIVE.`

segments.voice: Rehearse tonight: water on your hands and face, wudu or simply washing, then lying down on your right side. If you know al-Ikhlas, say it slowly in your mind, qul huwa Allahu ahad, and if you pray, plan for your last words to be bismika Allahumma amutu wa ahya, in Your name, O Allah, I die and I live. If you don't, choose one thing from today to set down before you sleep, and see yourself setting it down.
Adab of sleep. The manners of lying down: wudu, the right side, the three quls, and a last word of remembrance before the day lets go. Today's word.
Your line: sleep with remembrance. Each night a small dying, each morning a small rising. Tomorrow, the manners of learning.

1298.title: Adab of knowledge
1298.hook: a stranger in white sits knee to knee with the Prophet and teaches by asking
1298.howItsDone: Muslim students are taught to honor their teachers, to recite "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge," and to treat knowledge as something to act on, citing the hadith of Jibril and the hadith of what a person did with what they knew.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adab of sleep, and your line: sleep with remembrance. Today, the manners of learning, which is what this whole path has been doing.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab tells it, in Sahih Muslim. They were sitting with the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, when a man walked in. Very white clothes. Very black hair. No dust of travel on him, and nobody there knew who he was. He sat right in front of the Prophet, rested his knees against the Prophet's knees, laid his palms on his thighs, and began to ask questions. Only later did the Prophet tell them who it was. Jibril, the angel, come to teach them their religion. He taught by asking.
screen: `A STRANGER IN WHITE.` → `KNEE TO KNEE.` → `HE TAUGHT BY ASKING.`

segments.voice: That scene holds the adab of knowledge in its posture. Jibril came to teach, and he came looking like a student. He sat close. He was still. He asked, and listened. Respect for the one you learn from isn't flattery; it's how you sit. The Qur'an shows the same with a prophet. In al-Kahf, Moses meets a servant of Allah who has knowledge he doesn't, a man tradition calls al-Khidr. And Moses, himself a prophet, asks, in paraphrase: may I follow you, so that you can teach me some of the right guidance you've been taught? He's told he'll need patience. He agrees, and then struggles to keep quiet. In Ta Ha, the Prophet himself is told to ask for more, in Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." Nobody in these passages has finished learning. Then the sharp piece. Al-Saff, Pickthall again: "O ye who believe! Why say ye that which ye do not?" And a hadith in al-Tirmidhi says, in paraphrase, that on the Day of Rising a person's feet won't move until they're asked about their life, their wealth, their body, and their knowledge: what did you do with it? Not how much did you know. Knowledge, in this adab, isn't a collection. It's a debt paid in action.
screen: `A TEACHER WHO CAME AS A STUDENT.` · `A PROPHET ASKS TO FOLLOW.` · `MY LORD, INCREASE ME IN KNOWLEDGE.` · `WHAT DID YOU DO WITH IT?`

segments.voice: Look back over these last days, the kindlier word, the near side of the dish, leaving room, honoring the guest, the line before a trip, the last word before sleep, or anything else you've learned lately. Pick one you've heard and haven't yet done, and see exactly when it could happen. If you pray, you can say the line from Ta Ha: my Lord, increase me in knowledge.
Adab of knowledge. The manners of learning: honor the one who teaches, stay humble enough to ask for more, and act on what you know. Today's word.
Your line: learn, then do. Knowing is the start, not the finish. Same time tomorrow.

1299.title: Adab of the road
1299.hook: the companions want to keep sitting by the road, so they're told what the road is owed
1299.howItsDone: Muslims cite the hadith of the road's rights when teaching public manners, and treat lowering the gaze, returning salam and removing harm from the path as acts of faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adab of knowledge, and your line: learn, then do. Today, out the front door and onto the street.

Do roads have rights? A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says they do. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri reports that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, told his companions to avoid sitting along the roads. They pushed back. Those are our meeting places, they said. That's where we talk. So he didn't argue. He said, in paraphrase: if you must sit there, then give the road its right. And they asked the obvious next question. What is the road's right?
screen: `DO ROADS HAVE RIGHTS?` → `WE CAN'T HELP SITTING THERE.` → `THEN GIVE THE ROAD ITS RIGHT.`

segments.voice: His answer, in paraphrase: lowering the gaze, holding back harm, returning the greeting, and urging what is good while forbidding what is wrong. A street belongs to no one in particular, and that doesn't make it a free-for-all. Everyone on it is owed something by everyone else. First, the eyes. In al-Nur, in Pickthall's translation: "Tell the believing men to lower their gaze and be modest." The next verse says the same to the believing women. On a crowded street, a lowered gaze is a kind of privacy for people who can't close a door. Second, harm. Bukhari tells of a man who found a thorny branch lying across a road and moved it aside, and Allah thanked him for it and forgave him. One branch. And in Sahih Muslim, faith has many branches, the highest the declaration that there is no god but Allah, the lowest removing something harmful from the road. Even the lowest branch is still faith. Third, the greeting, from day three hundred eighty-four. Al-Nisa, Pickthall again: "When ye are greeted with a greeting, greet ye with a better than it or return it." It's owed back, and better if you can. And the last piece turns the sidewalk into a place where people look out for one another. The companions asked for permission to sit. What they got was a job.
screen: `A STREET OWES, AND IS OWED.` · `LOWER THE GAZE.` · `MOVE THE THORNY BRANCH.` · `RETURN THE GREETING, OR BETTER.`

segments.voice: Picture the street, hallway or parking lot you'll pass through next, and the people on it. Let your eyes come down gently where they don't need to wander, see your hand moving whatever's in the way, a bottle, a cart, a bag in the aisle, and hear yourself answering a greeting a little warmer than it came. If you pray, you can return a salam with wa 'alaykum al-salam.
Adab of the road. The manners of shared space: lower the gaze, hold back harm and clear it away, return the greeting, and urge the good. Today's word.
Your line: the road's rights. Even the lowest branch is still faith. See you at the market tomorrow.

1300.title: Adab of the market
1300.hook: a hand pushed into a heap of grain comes out wet
1300.howItsDone: Muslims are taught to trade by full measure, disclose a product's faults, avoid hoarding, and be easygoing when buying, selling and collecting debts, citing al-Mutaffifin and the hadith of the heap of grain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adab of the road, and your line: the road's rights. The street owes, and is owed.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is walking through the market, past a seller's heap of grain. He pushes his hand into it, deep, and his fingers come out wet. It's in Sahih Muslim. He asks the seller what this is. Rain got to it, the seller says. And the Prophet answers, in paraphrase: then why didn't you put the wet part on top, so people could see it? Then one short sentence about anyone who cheats, and it's the hardest line in today's lesson.
screen: `A HAND IN THE GRAIN.` → `WET UNDERNEATH.` → `WHY NOT PUT IT ON TOP?`

segments.voice: The sentence is: whoever cheats is not of me. Notice what the seller had done. He hadn't soaked the grain himself; rain did that. His fault was letting the dry grain hide the wet. In this adab, honesty has to be visible. The Qur'an says the same in the language of scales. Al-Mutaffifin, the defrauders, opens like this, in Pickthall's translation: "Woe unto the defrauders: Those who when they take the measure from mankind demand it full, But if they measure unto them or weigh for them, they cause them loss." Full measure when buying, short measure when selling: the verse catches the double standard. Then hoarding. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says, in paraphrase, that no one hoards except a sinner: buying up what people need and holding it back until they're desperate. The market is meant to feed people, not corner them. And the line this day is named for. In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: may Allah have mercy on a man who is easygoing when he sells, easygoing when he buys, and easygoing when he asks for what he's owed. The last, collecting a debt, is easy to skip. Another hadith in Bukhari: if buyer and seller are truthful and make things clear, their deal is blessed; if they hide things and lie, the blessing is wiped away. Honesty you can see, no profiting from need, and ease on both sides of the counter.
screen: `WHOEVER CHEATS IS NOT OF ME.` · `WOE UNTO THE DEFRAUDERS.` · `NO HOARDING.` · `EASY WHEN BUYING, SELLING, ASKING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one exchange coming up, a purchase, a bill, a refund, something you're selling, someone who owes you, and notice where you'd usually press hard, or grumble, or let the wet grain stay hidden. Now see it done the hadith's way: a fair price said plainly, any flaw said out loud, and a little more patience than you'd planned for whoever owes you. If you pray, you can ask for barakah, blessing, in your dealings.
Adab of the market. The manners of buying and selling: honest scales, nothing hidden, no hoarding, and ease when you sell, buy, and ask for what you're owed. Today's word.
Your line: easy in dealing. Honesty you can see. That's one thousand three hundred days.

1301.title: Adab with parents
1301.hook: a man asks who most deserves his good company, and hears one answer three times
1301.howItsDone: Muslims treat kindness to parents as a duty that follows worship of Allah, cite the hadith naming the mother three times, and recite "My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little" for their parents, living or dead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adab of the market, and your line: easy in dealing. Today, the adab closest to home.

Your mother. Then who? Your mother. Then who? Your mother. Then who? Then your father. Abu Hurayrah reports the exchange in Sahih al-Bukhari. A man had asked the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, which of all people most deserves his good companionship. He asked four times, and the answer didn't move until the fourth. Not a speech, not a list of virtues. One word, said again and again, until it couldn't be missed. Today's adab sits inside that repetition.
screen: `WHO MOST DESERVES MY COMPANY?` → `YOUR MOTHER. YOUR MOTHER. YOUR MOTHER.` → `THEN YOUR FATHER.`

segments.voice: Why say it three times? The hadith itself doesn't explain, but the Qur'an gives a picture. In surah Luqman, in Pickthall's translation: "His mother beareth him in weakness upon weakness." The verse goes on to the weaning. The repetition sounds like a debt counted out loud. And the father isn't dropped. He's named, and his place is real. Then how. In al-Isra, kindness to parents comes right after the command to worship none but Allah. When parents grow old, the verse says, don't even say uff to them, the smallest sound of irritation. Pickthall renders the rest: "speak unto them a gracious word." And the image of the wing: "lower unto them the wing of submission through mercy." A bird lowering its wing over its young; here the grown child does it for the parent. The verse gives a du'a too: "My Lord! Have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little." The adab has an honest edge. Surah Luqman says that if parents push a child to associate partners with Allah, the child shouldn't obey, but should still keep company with them kindly in this world. Disagreement doesn't cancel kindness. So adab with parents isn't only obedience. It's company, a gracious word, a lowered wing, and a du'a, with the mother named three times.
screen: `WEAKNESS UPON WEAKNESS.` · `NOT EVEN A SIGH OF IRRITATION.` · `THE WING LOWERED THROUGH MERCY.` · `DISAGREE, AND STAY KIND.`

segments.voice: Bring your mother to mind, or whoever mothered you, and if she's living and you can reach her, picture a call today and one gracious word you'd say. If she has died, a hadith in Sahih Muslim counts a child who prays for a parent among the good that continues after death; if you pray, you can say the line from al-Isra: my Lord, have mercy on them both as they did care for me when I was little. If the relationship is hard, simply hold her in mind with whatever mercy is possible today.
Adab with parents. Good companionship, gentle speech and a lowered wing of mercy, with the mother named three times before the father. Today's word.
Your line: mother, three times. And your father too. Tomorrow, the adab with neighbors.

1302.title: Adab with neighbors
1302.hook: an oath said three times, a pot of soup with extra water, and the people on the other side of the wall
1302.howItsDone: In Islamic teaching, kindness to neighbors is tied to faith, drawing on Qur'an 4:36 and hadith about keeping neighbors safe from harm and sharing food and small gifts with them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: adab with parents, the mother named three times, then the father. Today the circle widens by one wall, past the neighbor first met on day one hundred fifty-four.

By Allah, he does not believe. In paraphrase, those are the words, and the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said it once. Then again. Then a third time. Someone asked: who? In Sahih al-Bukhari, in paraphrase, his answer was: the one whose neighbor is not safe from his harm. Not a thief. Not a heretic. Someone living next door, whose neighbor has to stay a little on guard.
screen: `SAID ONCE. AGAIN. A THIRD TIME.` → `WHO?` → `THE ONE WHOSE NEIGHBOR ISN'T SAFE.`

segments.voice: Start with how high the Qur'an places the neighbor. In surah al-Nisa, verse thirty-six, in paraphrase, the command to worship Allah alone runs straight into a list of people owed kindness: parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, the neighbor who is kin, the neighbor who is a stranger, and the companion at your side. Worship and the house next door, in one breath. Then 'A'ishah's report, in Bukhari, in paraphrase: Gabriel kept urging me to be good to the neighbor, until I thought he would make the neighbor an heir. Then the oath from the hook, and what it asks: safety before generosity. The first thing a neighbor is owed is the absence of harm: no noise flung over the fence, no gossip, no dread when your door opens. Only then the giving, and the giving is small on purpose. In Sahih Muslim, in paraphrase, the Prophet told Abu Dharr: when you cook a broth, add more water, and look to your neighbors. A thinner soup, so it stretches one more house. And in Bukhari, in paraphrase, he told the women of the community: let no neighbor look down on a gift to her neighbor, even a sheep's hoof. So the adab comes in two steps. First, be someone the people beside you never have to brace for. Then, every so often, send something over. This week the manners of daily life have walked outward: the journey, the pillow, the teacher, the road, the market, your mother, and now the people closest to your walls.
screen: `AL-NISA: THE NEIGHBOR BESIDE WORSHIP.` · `GABRIEL KEPT URGING.` · `SAFE FROM YOUR HARM, FIRST.` · `MORE WATER IN THE SOUP.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people closest to where you live: through the wall, across the hall, down the road, some known by name, some only by their car or their light at night. For each, ask quietly: is this person safe beside me? Then pick one and picture a knock, or a word on the stairs; if you pray, hold that neighbor in your prayer.
Adab with neighbors. The manners owed to the people beside you: first, safety from your harm; then, a little more water in the pot. Today's word.
Your line: safe beside you. Safety comes first, and then the soup. Tomorrow, adab with children.
